questions.q: What is force?
questions.a: A push or a pull on an object, arising when two objects interact.

questions.q: Can force be seen? How do we know it acts?
questions.a: No - we infer it from its effects: moving, stopping, changing shape or direction of objects.

questions.q: Give two examples of force from daily life.
questions.a: Kicking a football (push) and opening a drawer (pull).

questions.q: How does a force arise from interaction?
questions.a: Two bodies must interact - touch or at a distance - for a force to act, like a magnet pulling a nail without contact.

questions.q: Give one example of contact force and one of non-contact force.
questions.a: Contact: muscular force or friction. Non-contact: gravity, magnetism, static electricity.

questions.q: Does a ball thrown upward keep rising forever? Why?
questions.a: No - the invisible force of gravity keeps pulling it down till it stops and falls.

questions.q: Currents push a boat with 90 N downstream and 65 N upstream. Compute the net force.
What is muscular force? Is it contact or non-contact?
questions.a: Force applied by muscles (walking, lifting); it is a contact force - the body must touch the object.

questions.q: Give two examples of muscular force.
questions.a: Chewing food and pushing a cycle pedal.

questions.q: Why must the force of an animal's muscles touch the object moved?
questions.a: Muscles act through limbs or body parts that press on the object, so contact is needed.

questions.q: What is friction?
questions.a: The force that opposes the sliding or rolling of one surface over another.

questions.q: Why does a rolling ball slow down and stop?
questions.a: Friction between the ball and ground, and with air, drains its motion energy.

questions.q: Name two ways friction is useful to us.
questions.a: It lets us walk without slipping, and lets brakes stop vehicles (also matches striking fire).

questions.q: What is electrostatic force?
questions.a: The force between charged bodies - a rubbed comb attracts paper bits without touching them.

questions.q: Is electrostatic force a contact force?
questions.a: No - it acts at a distance between charges.

questions.q: What happens when two similarly charged bodies meet?
questions.a: They repel each other; opposite charges attract.

questions.q: What is gravitational force?
questions.a: The attractive pull between any two bodies because of their mass - the earth pulls all objects toward itself.

questions.q: Why do fruits fall downward from trees?
questions.a: The earth's gravity pulls every object toward its centre.

questions.q: Does the moon also have gravity?
questions.a: Yes - the moon's gravity is about one-sixth of earth's, which raised tides and lets astronauts weigh less there.

questions.q: A force of 200 N acts on an area of 2 sq m. Find the pressure.
A 600 N box stands on a 0.5 sq m base. Calculate the pressure on the floor.
A nail tip of area 0.000001 sq m is hit with 20 N. Find the pressure at the tip.
A student of 400 N stands on both feet of total area 0.04 sq m. Compute the pressure.
A knife edge of area 0.0001 sq m cuts with 50 N. What pressure does it apply?
Why do liquids exert pressure on container walls?
questions.a: Liquid particles press in all directions due to their weight and motion.

questions.q: How does pressure of a liquid change with depth?
questions.a: It grows with depth - water columns at the bottom of a dam wall are thicker to bear it.

questions.q: Why do divers feel ear pain deep underwater?
questions.a: Water pressure rises with depth and presses on the eardrums.

questions.q: What is atmospheric pressure?
questions.a: The pressure the air around us exerts on every surface, about 100000 N per sq m at sea level.

questions.q: Why are we not crushed by atmospheric pressure?
questions.a: The pressure of fluids inside our bodies balances the outside air pressure.

questions.q: What holds a drinking straw's liquid up?
questions.a: Sucking lowers pressure in the straw; the atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface pushes the drink up.
